extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy; those studying Schopenhauer, ethics, and asceticism
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Schopenhauer's criteria for goodness, love, sympathy, and the denial of the will to live (asceticism). Useful for assessing moral character or texts about saintliness and ascetic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure love (αγαπη, caritas) is sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: All pure and disinterested love is sympathy; love which is not sympathy is selfishness (Έρως is selfishness, αγαπη is sympathy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True love consists in direct knowledge of and participation in others' suffering; sympathy is the core of genuine love. Combinations of selfish pleasure and sympathy frequently occur, but genuine love equals sympathy. Language, tones, and caresses of pure love coincide with those of sympathy; in some languages the same word denotes both (e.g., Italian pietà).

rubrics_metrics.name: Goodness and nobility arise from penetration of the principium individuationis
rubrics_metrics.description: Goodness of disposition and noble character spring from the lifting/penetration of the principle of individuation, which abolishes the egotistical distinction between self and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When one regards other individuals and their fate as equal to one's own, disinterested love and the capacity for supreme self-sacrifice follow. The truly noble will readily sacrifice personal well-being, even life, for the welfare of many (examples: Codrus, Leonidas, Regulus, Decius Mus, Arnold von Winkelried).

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue must proceed from sympathy, not from abstract reflection or duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine virtue results from felt sympathy and direct knowledge of others' suffering rather than from abstract concepts or the conception of duty (contra Kant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere concept is for genuine virtue as unfruitful as for genuine art; abstract reflection alone is insufficient. Felt sympathy, understood as knowledge of others' suffering placed on a level with one's own, is what influences people to good deeds and works of love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weeping as a sign of goodness and capacity for sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Weeping is not a direct expression of pain but sympathy with our own selves via imagination; it is conditional on capacity for love and imagination and is regarded as a sign of a certain degree of goodness of character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weeping often arises from reflecting one's pain as if it were another's and sympathising; those who are hard-hearted or unimaginative do not weep easily. Weeping disarms anger and indicates the continuing capacity for love and sympathy (e.g., children often cry only when someone commiserates them).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral action aims at alleviating suffering (satisfaction is removal of pain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suffering is essential to life; each wish proceeds from a want or suffering, and satisfaction is merely the removal of pain. Therefore goodness and love act primarily to alleviate suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All that can influence others to good deeds is knowledge of their suffering, directly understood from our own; the moral value of actions lies in their capacity to mitigate suffering, big or small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of the will to live (asceticism) as the highest ethical attainment
rubrics_metrics.description: The voluntary renunciation, resignation, and complete will-lessness — a turning away from life — is the culmination of the ethical development that begins with sympathy and goodness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the veil of individuation is lifted, one regards the world's infinite suffering as one's own and refrains from asserting life through volition. This manifests as horror of life's nature and leads to quieting of all volition and a settled indifference to worldly assertions of the will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascetic practices as evidence of denial of the will
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary chastity, intentional poverty, fasting, mortification of the body, self-inflicted suffering, accepting insult and injury without resistance, and general mortification of the will are practical signs of denying the will to live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such practices are not merely accidental or charitable but are ends in themselves intended to prevent pleasure and prosperity from rekindling the will. The ascetic welcomes suffering as confirmation that he no longer asserts the will and returns good for evil without ostentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saintliness judged by conduct rather than by doctrine or reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The conduct of a person — their lived denial of the will and moral deeds — certifies saintliness; it is irrelevant whether their explicit beliefs or dogmas are philosophically correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saints may hold the 'absurdest superstition' or be philosophers; what matters morally is their conduct. It is unreasonable to demand that a moralist teach only the virtue he personally possesses; philosophy (abstract knowledge) and saintliness (conduct) are distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuitive (in concreto) knowledge grounds virtue; abstract knowledge is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue proceeds from intuitive, direct knowledge of the world's nature rather than from abstract conceptual knowledge; philosophy's role is to make such knowledge explicit conceptually, but the will to act springs from intuition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Everyone is 'really conscious of all philosophical truths' intuitively; turning them into abstract concepts is the task of philosophy, but such abstract reflection by itself does not produce the moral conduct that springs from direct, in concreto apprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship mixes selfish pleasure and sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine friendship is typically a combination of selfish pleasure (the delight in a friend's presence) and sympathy (sincere participation in their joy and grief); selfishness often constitutes the greater part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that many moral relationships are mixed; the presence of some self-regarding pleasure does not negate the sympathy component, which shows itself in disinterested sacrifices and participation in others' suffering and joy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal compassion leads to taking on the world's suffering and withdrawal
rubrics_metrics.description: When one recognises the identity of will in all beings, all suffering becomes one's own; this comprehensive compassion can lead to an active horror of life and the decision to withdraw by denying further willing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains the progression from high goodness to asceticism: seeing the whole as suffering removes motives for asserting life and produces 'quieter' volition that culminates in will-lessness, often manifested historically in saints and ascetics across traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read biographies and lives of saints as practical illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract descriptions of the denial of the will are cold; to understand it fully one should study real-life examples in biographies of saints, ascetics, and penitents across cultures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend readings (e.g., lives of St. Francis, Christian mystics like Meister Eckhart, Indian Samanas, 'Autobiography of Madame de Guion') because practical examples better illustrate the intuitive knowledge and conduct described philosophically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-sacrifice for universal truth and welfare as noble action
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary submission to suffering or death in defence of universal truths and the welfare of mankind (not merely personal advantage) is a supreme expression of goodness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (Socrates, Giordano Bruno, martyrs) show that willingly facing certain death for friends, country, or truth is counted among the highest moral acts and follows from a character that places many others' welfare equal to or above one's own.
